metadata.title: How to Raise a Few Billion Dollars
metadata.guest_role: Chairman & President of Corporate Development, Lila Sciences; Author, The Tao of Fundraising

conclusion: Kim reframes fundraising as a trust craft, not a pitch deck sport: money moves at the speed of trust, persuasion equals desire minus fear, and belief is not enough if LPs still feel risk. His laws — differentiation over complexity, size-speed-terms trade-offs, and pipeline × conversion × bite size — explain how General Catalyst scaled into consensus capital and why logic-first pitches stall. The through-line is that great fundraisers operate like secretaries of state: they represent the firm when the principal is not in the room.
background:
Patrick talks with John Kim, formerly a prolific fundraiser at General Catalyst who helped turn the firm into one of the world's largest venture platforms, now chairman and president of corporate development at Lila Sciences (scientific superintelligence; $500M+ raised) and author of The Tao of Fundraising.

Kim would rename the book Money Moves at the Speed of Trust — the interim product of any fundraise is narrative and relationship, not IRR. The conversation covers friends-and-family as a hard-reelect base, consensus campaigns that move institutions, Oprah as a master of institutional trust mechanics, and why over-indexing on logos (logic) is the most common failure mode.
important_facts: Persuasion = desire − fear; belief ≠ trust: LPs can believe a plan is right and still not wire — Kim's skydiving/flying analogy. Friends-and-family is the hard-reelect base (trust already exists); first close often caps near 2× that base — a $1B first close tends to tap out around $2B. Start by mapping who desires your success more than they fear loss, then campaign outward.

Three physics laws of fundraising: (1) Differentiation = (track record + differentiation) ÷ complexity of story — complications destroy trust and kill internal advocates who cannot repeat the phrase. (2) Size, speed, and terms trade off — speed is really trust/scarcity; fake scarcity destroys credibility. (3) Pipeline math: pipeline × conversion ratio × bite size — once past hard-reelect, conversion ratio is the only lever that matters.

Consensus and courage: Institutional capital hides behind committees that almost never make contrarian bets — build consistency with pensions, consultants, and sovereigns until GC-style consensus forms, then have courage to lose early innovators who say you are too big. Differentiation requires sacrifice — firms that branded 'never weapons' then chased defense lost consistency and their why.

mental_model.name: Desire−Fear × Trust Velocity × Pipeline Conversion
mental_model.components: Desire and fear are emotional/ethical states; logic rationalizes a decision already felt. Trust is the last unlock after belief. Differentiation must be costly and consistent; complexity of story is the denominator. Campaigns convert a pipeline at a known ratio once the hard-reelect base is mapped. Consensus removes fear for committee capital but forces founders to abandon pure contrarian LP bases.
mental_model.application: Founders and GPs should audit every pitch for fear in the room, not just IRR slides. Improve conversion by sharpening track record, costly differentiation, and a repeatable one-liner. Never bluff scarcity. When scaling, decide whether size serves a real why — or prepare for the innovator's dilemma of losing early believers.

key_insights.view: Money moves at the speed of trust.
key_insights.question: Why do logical pitches still fail?
key_insights.answer: Belief gets you 'this makes sense'; trust gets the wire. People rationalize risk down rather than being truly risk-loving. Address fear and desire first — logos is the output of a successful meeting, not the input.

key_insights.question: How do scaled firms keep raising?
key_insights.answer: Find a durable why for size, not branding. Inconsistent mandates (e.g. never weapons → chase weapons) erase differentiation. Build consensus fund-by-fund with institutional reciprocity, then accept losing innovator LPs who need you small.

key_insights.question: Who should represent you?
key_insights.answer: Unlike cabinet roles with budget control, fundraising faces parties you cannot command — the first impression when you are not in the room must match the principal. Hire for that diplomatic trust, not pure sales energy.

top_investment_implications.thesis: Kim is now raising and structuring capital for scientific-superintelligence ambitions with $500M+ already raised — fundraising craft plus corporate-development seat signals serious institutional access into a high-capex AI-science bet

Kim's consensus-building playbook explains how GC scaled into large-pool venture — firms that intentionally convert innovator capital into institutional consensus capture durable AUM even as early LPs churn

golden_quotes: Money moves at the speed of trust.
Persuasion equals desire minus fear — belief is not trust.
